parts.title: Why Geese Fly South Together
paras: Long ago, when the world was new, geese did not fly south for the winter. Each goose did whatever it pleased. The most stubborn goose of all was a young gander named Toma. "I go where I want, when I want," he liked to say.

One fall, the leaves turned gold and the wind blew cold. Old Grandmother Goose gathered the flock beside the lake. "Snow is coming," she said. "Soon the lake will freeze, and the grass will be gone. We must fly south, where the water stays open and the plants still grow. We will fly together, so no one gets lost."

Toma flapped his wings and laughed. "Not me. This lake is my home, and I will not leave it." The flock begged him to come, but Toma would not change his mind. So the flock flew off without him, honking good-bye in a long line across the blue sky.

For a few days, Toma had the whole lake to himself. Then the snow came. It fell for three days and three nights. The lake turned to ice, so Toma had no place to swim. The grass was buried under the snow, so he had nothing to eat. Toma grew thin and weak. At night he shivered alone on the frozen shore.

One gray morning, a crow landed beside him. "Your flock went south," said the crow. "Follow the river. It will lead you to them." Toma was tired, but he flew and flew along the river. Each day he flew a little slower. At last he heard honking. His flock was resting on a warm, open lake. Grandmother Goose spread her wings around him. "We knew you would come," she said.

Toma never forgot that hard winter. The next fall, he was the first goose to line up. And that is why, to this day, geese fly south together in a long V across the sky, calling to one another so that no one is left behind.

parts.title: On the Move: How Geese Migrate
paras: Every fall, you may hear loud honking high above you. Look up, and you might see a flock of Canada geese flying in the shape of a V. The geese are migrating. To migrate means to travel from one place to another when the seasons change.

Geese eat grass, seeds, and water plants. In winter, snow covers the ground and ponds freeze in many northern places. When food is hard to find, many geese fly south, where the weather is warmer and the water stays open. In spring, when the snow melts, they fly back north to raise their babies, called goslings.

Migrating geese often fly in a V shape. Scientists think the V helps the birds save energy. Each goose flies a little behind and to the side of the goose in front of it, where moving air helps lift its wings. Flying at the front is the hardest job, so the geese take turns leading. Their honking helps the flock stay together.

How do geese know where to go? Young geese learn the route by flying with their parents. Scientists believe geese also use the sun, the stars, and landmarks such as rivers, coastlines, and mountains to find their way.

Not all Canada geese migrate. In many towns and cities, including parts of Virginia, some geese stay all year long. Parks, ponds, and golf courses give them grass to eat and water that does not freeze. Because they can find food in winter, they do not need to make the long trip.

parts.title: Marla Barnes and the Mighty Storm
paras: Up in the hills of Virginia, on a farm with a red barn, lived the strongest girl who ever wore boots. Her name was Marla Barnes. On the day she was born, she let out a yell so loud that it shook the apples off every tree in the orchard. Her first word was "MORE!" and she said it to her mother's corn bread.

By the time she was five, Marla could carry a cow under each arm. By the time she was eight, she could plow the whole cornfield before breakfast, using a fork from the kitchen. Folks came from miles around just to watch her work, and they always left shaking their heads.

One hot summer, a storm started to grow far out past the mountains. It was the biggest, fiercest storm anyone had ever seen. Its clouds were as dark as a barn at midnight, and its thunder roared so loud that the stars hid. The storm was heading straight for Marla's town.

The people of the town met in the town hall to decide what to do. Some wanted to hide in their cellars. Some wanted to pack their carts and run. Everybody talked at once, and nobody could agree. Finally, Marla stood up. "Let's vote," she said. "Each person gets one vote, and the idea with the most votes wins." The people wrote their choices on scraps of paper and dropped them into a hat. When the votes were counted, most people had chosen Marla's idea: she would stop the storm herself.

Marla marched to the top of the tallest hill. The storm roared toward her, spinning faster than a top. Marla did not run. She reached up, grabbed the storm by its tail, and tied it in a knot. Then she swung onto its back and rode it like a wild horse.

The storm bucked and twisted for three days and three nights. It tore so hard at the ground that it scooped out a valley, and the valley filled with rain and became a lake. At last the storm grew tired. Marla steered it to the seashore and set it gently down over the ocean, where it turned into a soft, warm rain.

When Marla came home, the whole town cheered. They voted again, and this time every single vote said the same thing: Marla Barnes was the town's hero. If you visit those hills today, you can still swim in the lake that the storm dug, the summer Marla Barnes rode it out to sea.

parts.title: Every Vote Counts: How Voting Works
paras: Imagine your class has to choose a name for its new fish. Some students want Bubbles. Others want Captain Fin. How can the class decide in a fair way? One fair way is to vote. When people vote, each person gets one choice, and the choice with the most votes wins.

In the United States, adults choose many of their leaders by voting. Citizens who are 18 years old or older can vote for leaders such as the president, the governor of their state, and the mayor of their town. People also vote on questions, such as whether their town should build a new park. Election Day is the Tuesday after the first Monday in November.

On Election Day, many voters go to a polling place, such as a school or a library. Each voter gets a ballot. A ballot is a paper or a screen that lists the choices. The voter marks one choice for each question. In many states, including Virginia, people can also vote early or mail in their ballot.

Voting is private. Each voter marks the ballot alone, behind a screen or curtain, and no one else sees the choices. Because the vote is secret, people can choose what they really think without worrying that someone will be upset with them.

After the polls close, workers count the ballots carefully. The choice with the most votes wins. When a choice gets more than half of all the votes, we say it has a majority. Sometimes an election is very close, and just a few votes make the difference. That is why people say every vote counts.

parts.title: Shirley Burke Digs a River
paras: In the dry hill country there once lived a girl named Shirley Burke. She was so quick that she could turn off the light and be in bed before the room got dark. Her curly hair was so thick that birds built nests in it, and she never minded one bit. She could whistle louder than a train, and she once outran a jackrabbit just to say good morning.

One summer, no rain fell for forty days. The sun burned the grass brown, and the dirt cracked into a thousand pieces. The town well went dry. The cows in Farmer Hurd's herd were so thirsty that they mooed in a whisper, and even the frogs packed their bags and hopped away.

The town council met to solve the problem. The council members talked about digging a new well, but the ground was as hard as rock. They talked about carrying water from the Silver River, but the river was a three-day walk away. No one could think of a plan that would work.

Then Shirley spoke up at the meeting. "If the town can't go to the river," she said, "I'll bring the river to the town." The council members laughed, but Shirley did not. She rolled up the sleeves of her shirt, picked up a shovel, and started to dig.

Shirley dug so fast that dirt flew up like a fountain. Rocks, roots, and old stumps leaped out of her way. In the first hour she dug a mile. By sunset she had dug all the way to the Silver River. When she lifted her last shovelful, the river burst through with a roar and came rushing down her ditch, curving and turning all the way to town.

The people cheered and splashed. Farmer Hurd's cows drank until their bellies were as round as barrels. The council voted to name the new river after Shirley, and they made a new rule: no one may ever waste a single drop of its water.

That is why, if you visit the dry hill country today, you will find a river with more twists and turns than a curly ribbon. People say it curves because Shirley stopped to say hello to every family on her way to town. Some folks say that on hot summer evenings, you can still hear Shirley humming as the water rushes by.

parts.title: Who Makes the Rules in Your Town?
paras: Every community has rules. Some rules tell drivers how fast they may go. Others say when the library is open or where dogs must wear a leash. Rules made by a government are called laws. Who makes the laws for a town?

In many towns, a group of people called the town council makes local laws. The people of the town vote to choose the council members. The council meets in public, often once or twice a month, to talk about problems and decide what to do.

Many towns also have a mayor. The mayor leads the town and works with the council. In some places the mayor runs the council meetings and helps plan how the town will spend its money. The mayor also speaks for the town at special events, such as the opening of a new library.

First, someone notices a problem, such as cars driving too fast near a school. Next, the council talks about the problem at a meeting and listens to what citizens think. Then the council members vote on a new rule, such as a lower speed limit. If the rule passes, the town puts up signs so everyone knows about it.

Council meetings are open to the public. Citizens can come to a meeting, share their ideas, and ask questions. Even kids can write a letter to the council. When citizens speak up, leaders learn what the community needs.

texts.title: Joy Howard and the Voice That Saved the Town

parts.title: Joy Howard and the Voice That Saved the Town
paras: In a little town by the sea lived a girl named Joy Howard, and Joy had the loudest voice in the world. When she was a baby, her cry could knock the crows out of the trees. When she sang in the shower, the fish in the bay popped their heads out of the water to listen. Her laugh was so big that it once blew the hat off the mailman two streets away.

Joy's voice made some people grumble. "Joy, please don't shout," her mother would say. "Use your inside voice." Joy tried. She whispered, she murmured, and she mumbled. But even Joy's whisper could rattle the windows on Main Street, and her mumble could be heard in the next town.

One autumn night, a thick fog rolled in from the ocean. It was so thick you could cut it with a spoon. Out at sea, the fishing boats were heading home, but the fishermen could not see the shore. They called out to one another, but they could barely see the ends of their own boats. To make matters worse, the town's foghorn had broken that very morning. Without the horn, the boats might crash into the rocks.

The mayor ran through the town looking for help. "Somebody has to call the boats home!" she cried. People shouted from the docks, but the fog swallowed their voices. Then the mayor remembered Joy Howard.

Joy climbed to the top of the lighthouse. She took a deep breath, all the way down to her toes, and she shouted, "THIS WAY HOME!" Her voice boomed across the water like a giant drum. It bounced off the clouds and rolled over the waves. Out in the fog, the fishermen heard it. They turned their boats toward the sound and followed it, one by one, safely into the harbor.

The next day, the whole town gathered in front of the town hall. The mayor gave Joy a shiny brass crown that said Official Town Voice. Joy wore it every day. From then on, nobody asked Joy to use her inside voice, and whenever the fog rolled in, she climbed the lighthouse stairs two at a time. And on foggy nights, sailors say you can still hear her calling across the bay.

parts.title: Lights and Horns: How Lighthouses Keep Sailors Safe
paras: For hundreds of years, sailors have faced a big danger near the shore: rocks hidden under the water. At night or in a storm, a ship could crash before the crew ever saw land. Lighthouses were built to warn sailors and guide them safely home.

A lighthouse is a tall tower with a bright light at the top. Lighthouses stand on rocky points, on islands, and at the edges of harbors. Because the tower is so tall, sailors can see its light from many miles away. Many lighthouses are also painted with bright stripes or patterns so sailors can spot them in the daytime.

Each lighthouse flashes its light in its own pattern. One might flash every five seconds. Another might flash twice and then go dark. By counting the flashes, sailors can tell which lighthouse they are looking at and figure out where they are.

Thick fog can hide even the brightest light. So many lighthouses also had a fog signal, such as a bell or a foghorn. The loud, low sound traveled through the fog and warned sailors that land was near.

Long ago, lighthouse keepers lived at the lighthouse. Every night they climbed the stairs to light the lamp, and they polished the glass so the light would shine brightly. Today most lights turn on by themselves, and ships also use computers and satellites to find their way. One of the oldest lighthouses in the country, the Old Cape Henry Lighthouse, was finished in 1792 and still stands in Virginia Beach.

parts.title: Fern Thornbury and the Night of the Frost
paras: In the valley town of Cornfield Corners lived a farmer named Fern Thornbury, the tallest, strongest farmer anyone had ever seen. When she was a baby, she used a barn door for a blanket. By the time she was ten, she could plow a whole field with a soup spoon before breakfast. When she needed to blow her nose, she just reached up and borrowed a cloud.

Fern's farm grew the biggest crops in the county. Her corn grew so tall that birds needed a rest stop halfway up. Every fall her harvest was plentiful, with more food than her barn could hold, so Fern shared the extra with her neighbors.

One October afternoon, a sharp wind began to blow from the north. Old Farmer Burke sniffed the air and frowned. "Frost tonight," he said. "A hard one. By morning, every crop in the valley will be frozen solid." Twenty farms needed picking, and daylight was almost gone.

Mayor Rosa Garcia rang the big bell in front of the town hall, and the town council hurried inside for a meeting. "Fern can pick corn faster than fifty people," said one council member. The council voted, and the plan was simple: Fern would bring in the harvest before the frost arrived.

Fern got to work. She twisted ten ears of corn off their stalks at a time. She tossed pumpkins into her wagon as if they were tennis balls. Her boots stomped so hard that the soil puffed up in little clouds of dust. By sundown, three whole farms were finished.

But the night grew colder, and seventeen farms were still left. Fern's arms began to ache. For the first time in her life, Fern felt weary. She was so tired that she could barely lift a single pumpkin. She sat down on a hay bale, and for once she did not feel tall at all.

Just then, she saw lights bobbing down the road. Her neighbors were coming with lanterns, baskets, and wheelbarrows, with Mayor Garcia in front. Grandparents pulled corn from the stalks. Children made a long line and passed pumpkins from hand to hand, all the way to the barn doors.

When the sun came up, the frost sparkled on the empty fields like sugar on a cookie. Every pumpkin and every ear of corn was safe inside a barn. The mayor tried to give Fern a shiny medal, but Fern shook her head. "Give it to the whole town," she said with a laugh. "I may be tall, but my neighbors carried us through the night."

So the council held one more vote. From then on, Cornfield Corners held a Harvest Thank-You Supper every fall, at one long table down the middle of Main Street. Everyone came to enjoy the food and say thank you. Fern always sat at the very end, because her legs were so long that her feet poked into the next county.

parts.title: Serving the Community: How a Town Takes Care of Its People
paras: Who fixes the holes in the road on your street? Who makes sure the fire trucks are ready and the library stays open? In most places, the answer is the local government. A local government is a group of leaders who serve the people of one town, city, or county. Its job is to take care of the things that everyone in the community shares.

In many towns and cities, voters choose a mayor and a group called a council. The mayor leads the town, a little like the captain of a team. The council members meet to talk about problems and vote on plans. In Virginia, each county has a similar group called a board of supervisors. These leaders are elected, which means the people pick them by voting.

A service is a job done to help people. Local governments run many services. They pay firefighters to put out fires and police officers to keep people safe. They take care of parks, playgrounds, and libraries. Many towns also fix roads and keep the traffic lights working. In many places, they also collect trash and clean the streets.

All of these services cost money. Most of the money comes from taxes, which are amounts of money that people and businesses pay to the government. Sharing the cost lets a town buy a fire truck that one family could never afford. Then the truck is ready to help anyone in town who needs it.

Council meetings are usually open to the public, so anyone can come and listen. At many meetings, people may stand up and share their ideas. Suppose a neighbor notices that a busy corner has no crosswalk. First, she tells the council about the problem. The council talks it over and votes on a plan. Then a work crew paints a new crosswalk on the corner. Speaking up is one way people help their town.

A town does not take care of its people with leaders alone. Neighbors help too. Many people volunteer, which means they work for free to help others. parts.title: Raccoon and the Moon in the Brook
paras: Long ago, a raccoon lived beside Hollow Brook. Raccoon had sharp eyes, quick paws, and a very big appetite. Every autumn, when the pawpaw trees dropped their soft green fruit, Raccoon wanted to hoard every single one, keeping all of them for himself.

"These pawpaws are mine," he told the other animals. He dragged the fallen fruit into a giant pile under his tree. By day he added more to the pile, and by night he slept on top of it. Squirrel, Possum, and the fox kits could only watch with rumbling bellies. Raccoon would not share even one bite.

Turtle saw all of this from her log in the brook. She was small and slow, but her mind was as quick as a minnow. One cool evening, she crawled up to the pile. "Good evening, Raccoon," she said. "Have you heard about the golden pawpaw? It is bigger than all of your pawpaws put together."
Raccoon's ears perked up. "Where is it?" he asked.
"In the brook," said Turtle. "It only comes when the sky is dark. If you want it, you must stay by the water all night." Raccoon licked his lips. A pawpaw that big could fill him up until spring.

That night, the full moon rose over the trees. Its reflection, the picture of the moon shining back from the water, lay on the brook like a round, glowing fruit. Raccoon gasped. He reached in with both paws and grabbed. Splash! The golden pawpaw broke into a hundred wiggly pieces. Raccoon waited, and slowly the pieces floated back together. He grabbed again. Splash!

All night long, Raccoon patted and poked and felt around in the cold water. He never once looked back at his pile. Meanwhile, Turtle quietly called the other animals. Squirrel, Possum, and the fox kits hauled away the pawpaws one by one and shared them with every hungry family in the woods.

When the sun came up, the golden pawpaw faded away. Raccoon gave a huge yawn and trudged home with soggy fur, his feet dragging with every slow, heavy step. His giant pile was gone. Only one pawpaw was left, sitting on a flat rock beside Turtle. "We saved you one," Turtle said. "Sharing means everyone gets some."
Raccoon frowned. Then his stomach growled, and he laughed in spite of himself. "Well," he said, "one pawpaw I can eat is better than a moon I cannot catch."
Raccoon never caught the golden pawpaw. But to this day, raccoons still go down to the water at night and feel around with their clever paws, just in case it comes back.

texts.title: Masked Night Visitors: All About Raccoons

parts.title: Masked Night Visitors: All About Raccoons
paras: Raccoons have lived in the forests of North America for a very long time, and they star in many old stories. Today you can find them in woods, wetlands, farms, and even big cities. They live in every part of Virginia. The name raccoon comes from a word in the Powhatan language, which was spoken by Native American people in Virginia long ago.

It is easy to spot a raccoon. Its fur is mostly gray and brown. Dark fur around its eyes looks like a mask, and its bushy tail has several dark rings. Some scientists think the dark mask may cut down on glare, the bright light that can make it hard to see. A grown raccoon is about the size of a small dog.

A raccoon's front paws look a little like tiny hands, with five long fingers. They are very sensitive, which means they can feel even the smallest bumps. Raccoons often dip their food in water and rub it with their paws. It looks like washing, but scientists think wet paws may help raccoons feel their food better. Raccoons are so good with their paws that some have even learned to open simple latches and lids.

Raccoons are omnivores. An omnivore is an animal that eats both plants and animals. In the summer and autumn, raccoons eat berries, grapes, acorns, and pawpaws. They also catch crayfish, frogs, and insects, and they will even eat bird eggs. Raccoons often hunt for food in streams by feeling under rocks with their paws.

Raccoons are nocturnal, which means they are awake at night and sleep during the day. At dusk, when the sky begins to grow dark, they leave their dens to look for food. During the day, many raccoons rest in a den, such as a hollow tree. When the weather gets very cold, raccoons may sleep in their dens for days at a time, but they do not truly hibernate.

In towns and cities, raccoons sometimes knock over trash cans to look for food. People can keep raccoons away by putting tight lids on their cans and bringing pet food inside at night. Raccoons are wild animals, so it is best to watch them from far away and never feed them.

parts.title: The Night I Was Tricked (as Told by Raccoon)
paras: Everyone in these woods tells the story of the night Turtle tricked me. They tell it while they are baking acorn cakes, and they tell it while they are raking leaves. They always get it wrong. I am Raccoon, and I was there, so I will tell you what really happened.

It was autumn, and I had saved a pile of pawpaws under my tree. Yes, it was a big pile. But I was not being greedy. I was storing food for winter, the way any smart animal does. Squirrel hides acorns, and nobody calls him greedy.

One evening, Turtle came sliding up from the brook, smiling her slow little smile. She told me about a golden pawpaw that floated in the water at night. I was sure she was joking, because turtles love to tease. Still, I wanted to see for myself.

That night, the full moon was shining over the trees. I sat by the brook, and there it was: a round, glowing shape in the water. The others say I grabbed at it again and again like a silly kit. That is not true. I was washing my paws, which is what tidy raccoons do before a big meal.

Every time I dipped my paws in, the golden shape broke into a hundred shivering pieces, like a plate dropped on a stone. Then the pieces slid back together. I will admit that this was puzzling. I could not figure it out at all. I patted the water. I poked it. Was I hoping to catch it? Maybe a little.
By the time the sky turned pink, my fur was soaked and my paws were as wrinkled as old leaves. I yawned and walked home, dripping with every step. And that is when I saw it. My pile was gone.

For a moment, my heart dropped into my muddy feet. Then I heard laughing. Through the trees I saw Squirrel, Possum, and the fox kits sitting in a circle. They were sharing my pawpaws with every family in the woods.

Turtle waved me over. She had saved one pawpaw for me on a flat rock. I wanted to be angry. I truly did. But the kits looked so happy, and I was so very hungry. I sat down and ate my pawpaw beside them. It was the best one I have ever tasted, maybe because I was not eating it alone.

So that is the true story. The others say I was tricked. I say I was taught. I still go down to the brook at night to wash my paws and look at the moon. But these days, when autumn comes, I make a smaller pile, and I share it.

texts.label: Fact text
texts.title: Why Does the Moon Change Shape?

parts.title: Why Does the Moon Change Shape?
paras: Have you ever noticed that the moon looks different from night to night? Some nights it is a round, shining circle. Other nights it is a thin curve, like a slice of melon. Some nights you cannot see it at all. The moon is not really changing its shape, though. Something else is going on.

The moon does not make any light of its own. It is a huge, rocky ball with no fire and no lamps. Astronauts who walked on the moon found gray dust and rocks, not glowing stones. The light we see is sunlight bouncing off the moon's surface. The side of the moon facing the sun is bright, and the side facing away is dark. It is a little like holding a ball near a flashlight in a dark room.

The moon travels around Earth. As it moves, we see different amounts of its sunny side, and it takes about 29 and a half days to go through all of its shapes. These shapes are called phases. When the moon is between Earth and the sun, its bright side faces away from us. This is the new moon, and it is very hard to see. About two weeks later, the moon is on the far side of Earth, and we can see its whole sunny side. This is the full moon, and it shines brightly all night long.

After the new moon, a thin curve of light appears. Night after night, the bright part grows bigger. People say the moon is waxing, or growing. After the full moon, the bright part gets smaller each night until it is gone again. People say the moon is waning, or shrinking. Then the pattern starts over, so you can predict what the moon will look like next week.

On a calm, clear night, you may see the moon in a pond or lake. This is a reflection. The moon's light bounces off the smooth water and into your eyes, so the moon seems to be floating right there. If you drop a pebble in, the reflection breaks into wiggly pieces. When the water becomes still again, the pieces come back together. On a windy night, little ripples can make the reflection shiver and shake. The real moon, of course, is about 239,000 miles away.

parts.title: How Hare Got Her Winter Coat
paras: Long ago, when the world was new, Hare was brown all year long. Her feet were small and neat, and in summer she was quick and happy. She went hopping through the green grass, nibbling clover and sunning herself on warm rocks.

But every winter, Hare had a problem. When the snow came, her small feet sank deep into the drifts, and she kept slipping and tumbling. Worse, her brown fur showed against the white snow like a raisin on a plate of rice. Fox could spot her from across the meadow.
"I love winter," Fox said, grinning and licking his lips. "Everything is so easy to see." Hare did not love winter at all. She spent the cold months hiding under bushes, shivering and hungry.

One gray morning, Hare heard someone grumbling in the woods. An old woman in a long white cloak was digging in a snowbank. Her hair was as white as frost, and tiny snowflakes drifted from her sleeves whenever she moved. It was Grandmother Winter herself.
"I dropped my mittens," Grandmother Winter said with a sigh. "Without them, I cannot make the snow fall softly. It will come down hard and icy instead."

Hare's feet were small, but they were good for digging. She started right away, flinging snow behind her. She dug for a long time, and her paws grew numb with cold until she could hardly feel them. She thought about stopping. Then she thought about icy snow covering all the little animals of the forest, and she kept going. At last, she felt something soft. She pulled out two fluffy white mittens.
Grandmother Winter clapped her hands, and a shower of snowflakes swirled into the air. "You have a kind heart and a strong will," she said. "Ask me for a gift."
Hare thought carefully. "I wish I could walk on top of the snow," she said, "and I wish Fox could not see me so easily."

Grandmother Winter smiled. She touched Hare's back feet, and they grew long and wide and fuzzy, like two little snowshoes. Then she brushed her cloak across Hare's fur, and the brown turned as white as the snow. "Every winter you will wear white," she said, "and every spring your brown coat will return."

That afternoon, Fox came trotting across the meadow, looking for Hare. He passed right by her and never noticed a thing. Hare sat very still, trying not to giggle. Then she went running off across the snow, her big feet carrying her along without sinking at all.
And that is why, to this day, the snowshoe hare changes her coat when the snow comes.

parts.title: Snowshoe Hares: Dressed for Winter
paras: In the snowy forests of Canada, Alaska, and the northern United States lives an animal with clever ways to survive the winter. It is the snowshoe hare. A snowshoe hare looks like a large rabbit, with long ears and strong back legs. Hares are close cousins of rabbits, but they are not quite the same.

The snowshoe hare gets its name from its huge back feet. Each foot is long and wide, and in winter, thick fur grows between the toes. These big, furry feet spread out the hare's weight, the same way snowshoes help a person walk on deep snow without sinking. The hare can go hopping across soft snow while heavier animals sink in. When it needs to escape, it can leap about 10 feet in a single jump.

In summer, a snowshoe hare's fur is brown. In fall, the hare starts shedding its brown fur, and white fur grows in its place. By the time the snow is deep, the hare is almost all white, except for dark tips on its ears. This camouflage, or coloring that helps an animal blend in, makes it hard for foxes, lynx, and owls to spot the hare. In spring, the hare turns brown again.

What tells the hare when to change? Scientists have learned that the change is set off mostly by the length of the day. As the days grow shorter in fall, the hare's body begins making white fur. This can cause trouble when snow comes late. A white hare sitting on brown ground is easy to see.

In summer, snowshoe hares eat grasses, clover, and flowers. Winter is harder, because those plants are buried under snow. Then the hares nibble on twigs, buds, and bark from bushes and small trees. Hares do not sleep through the winter. They stay busy all season, mostly feeding at night and resting in sheltered spots during the day.

Baby hares are called leverets. Baby rabbits are born without fur and with their eyes shut. Leverets are different. They are born with fur and with their eyes open, and within a day or so, they can start hopping around.

parts.title: Louis Braille: Reading with Fingertips
paras: In 1809, a baby boy named Louis Braille was born in Coupvray, a small village not far from Paris, France. His father made harnesses and saddles for horses, and his workshop was full of leather straps and sharp tools. Little Louis loved to watch his father work. He liked the rich smell of the leather and the tap, tap, tap of the hammer.

When Louis was about three years old, he was playing in the workshop when a sharp tool slipped and hurt one of his eyes. Doctors in those days did not have the medicines we have today. An infection spread to his other eye, and by the time he was about five, Louis could not see at all.

Louis did not let blindness stop him from learning. He went to the village school with the other children and listened closely to every lesson. But he could not read books by himself. To Louis, every printed page was like a locked door. Books were full of stories, and he wanted to open them on his own.

When he was ten, Louis won a place at a special school for blind students in Paris. The school had books with big raised letters that students could feel with their fingers. However, the letters were hard to tell apart, and the books were huge and heavy. One story could fill several thick volumes, or separate books. The school owned only a small number of them, so students had very little to read.

When Louis was about twelve, a visitor came to the school. Charles Barbier, a former army captain, had invented a way to write with raised dots. Some say he hoped it would let soldiers read messages in the dark without a light. Barbier's system was clever, but it was cumbersome, or hard to use, because one sound could need as many as twelve dots. A fingertip could not feel all of those dots at once.

Louis liked the idea of dots, but he knew it had to be simpler. He worked on it for about three years, late at night and even during school vacations at home. He tried many patterns. Some were too big, and some were confusing. At last, when he was about fifteen, he finished a system that used just six dots in two short columns. Each pattern stood for a letter, a number, or a mark like a comma. Because one fingertip could cover all six dots, readers could move quickly across a line.

The other students loved the new system, because they could finally read and write on their own. Louis later became a teacher at the school, and he even added patterns for writing music. Still, many adults were slow to accept the dots. The school did not officially adopt Louis's system, or choose it as the one to use, until 1854. That was two years after Louis died.

Today, braille is used in many countries and in many languages. You can find it on elevator buttons, signs, and menus, and libraries lend braille books to families everywhere. A boy who once had almost nothing to read gave millions of people a way to read stories with their fingertips.

texts.label: Fact text
texts.title: Every Invention Starts with a Problem

parts.title: Every Invention Starts with a Problem
paras: Look around the room you are in. The pencil, the light switch, and the zipper on your jacket were all invented by someone. Most inventions do not begin with a big idea. They begin with a problem. An inventor notices that something is hard, slow, or annoying and wonders how it could work better. Then the inventor gets to work.

Inventors are good observers, which means they pay close attention to the world around them. In 1902, a woman from Alabama named Mary Anderson visited New York City in winter. Streetcars carried people around many big cities then. As she rode one on a snowy day, she noticed that the driver kept opening his window to wipe snow and ice off the glass. Cold air rushed in, and he still could not see well.

Next, an inventor thinks of ways to solve the problem. Mary Anderson designed an arm with a rubber blade that swept across the outside of the window. The driver could move it with a handle from inside. In 1903, she received a patent for her idea. A patent is a paper from the government that says an invention belongs to the person who made it, so others cannot copy it without permission.

Few inventions work perfectly the first time. Inventors build a model, test it, find what goes wrong, and try again. Some tests fail, but each one teaches the inventor something new. Many inventions also grow from someone else's idea. Early wipers had to be moved by hand. Later, other inventors improved the idea so that wipers could run by themselves. Today, almost every car has them.

Sometimes nature points the way to a solution. In the 1940s, a Swiss engineer named George de Mestral came home from a walk and found burrs stuck to his clothes and to his dog's fur. Burrs are small, prickly seed pods. He looked at one under a microscope and saw hundreds of tiny hooks. After years of work, he invented a fastener with tiny hooks on one strip and soft loops on the other. Today, fasteners like his close shoes, jackets, and backpacks.

Kids can be inventors, too. Think about the problems in your own life, and ask your family and friends what bugs them, too. Maybe your marker caps keep getting lost, or the straps on your bag keep slipping. Write down the problem, sketch some ideas, and build a simple model. Your solution might make many people's days a little easier.

Dear Pencil, you're yellow and skinny and tall,
With six little sides so you won't roll and fall.
You sleep in my backpack, tucked into your case,
Then wake up for school with a grin on your face.

You've written my stories of dragons and kings,
Of puppies with jet packs and cities with wings.

When I make a mistake, you just flip upside down,

Too tiny to hold and too short to stand.

parts.title: The Surprising Story of the Pencil
paras: It is one of the simplest tools in your classroom, and you probably use it every day. You might not think about it at all. But the pencil has a long and surprising history. It took hundreds of years, and the ideas of many different people, to make the pencil we know today.

Many people call the inside of a pencil its "lead," but pencils have no lead in them at all. The dark gray center is made of graphite, a soft mineral that leaves a mark when you rub it on paper. In the 1500s, people in Borrowdale, England, found a large amount of graphite in the ground. It looked a lot like lead, a gray metal, so people called it lead. The name stuck, even though it was wrong.

At first, people simply carried chunks of graphite or wrapped them in string. Some stories say that shepherds in Borrowdale used it to mark their sheep. Graphite is soft and messy, so it left gray smudges on people's fingers. Later, people began placing thin sticks of graphite inside pieces of wood. The wood kept hands clean and made the graphite easier to hold. This was the beginning of the wooden pencil.

In the 1790s, a French inventor named Nicolas-Jacques Conté found a new way to make pencil centers. He mixed powdered graphite with clay and baked the mixture in an oven. More clay made a harder pencil with a lighter line. More graphite made a softer pencil with a darker line. Pencil makers still use this idea today. The number printed on a pencil, such as 2, tells how hard or soft it is.

For a long time, people erased mistakes with a separate piece of rubber, or even with a lump of bread. In 1858, an American named Hymen Lipman received a patent for a pencil with an eraser attached to one end. Now the eraser could not get lost. An eraser works because the rubber grabs tiny bits of graphite and lifts them off the paper. Most pencils sold in the United States still have an eraser on top.

Today, factories make billions of pencils every year. Many pencils have six sides, which keeps them from rolling off desks. Artists use soft pencils to draw dark shadows, and builders use flat pencils that will not roll away. A pencil can even write upside down. Not bad for a tool made of wood, clay, and a little gray mineral!

parts.title: Garrett Morgan: Making Streets Safer
paras: Garrett Morgan was born in 1877 in Paris, Kentucky. He grew up on a farm, one of eleven children in a busy family. Like many children at that time, he had to leave school early to work, after about the sixth grade. But Garrett never stopped learning. He loved to figure out how things worked.

As a teenager, Garrett moved north to Ohio to find work. He settled in Cleveland, a fast-growing city full of factories. He got a job fixing sewing machines, and he was good at it. He could take a broken machine apart, find the problem, and put it back together so it ran smoothly. He even hired a tutor, a teacher who worked with him alone, to help him keep learning to read and write well.

In 1907, Garrett opened his own repair shop. Later, he and his wife, Mary Anne, opened a tailor shop where workers sewed coats, suits, and dresses. The business did well. Garrett was proud of it, but his mind was always busy with new ideas.

One of those ideas was a safety hood. Firefighters often had trouble breathing in thick smoke. Garrett's hood fit over a person's head and had a long tube that hung down near the ground, where the air was cleaner. He received a patent for it in 1914.

Two years later, his invention was put to a real test. In 1916, workers were trapped in a tunnel deep under Lake Erie after an accident filled it with smoke and gas. Garrett and his brother Frank rushed to the lake in the middle of the night. They pulled on safety hoods and went down into the tunnel, and they helped carry men out. At first, Garrett did not get much credit for his bravery, but many people in Cleveland never forgot it.
Garrett bought a car when cars were still new. Back then, and the streets were crowded with cars, horse-drawn wagons, bicycles, and people on foot. Many busy corners had no signals at all.

Many stories say that Garrett saw a crash between a car and a horse-drawn carriage at one of those corners. Whether or not it happened just that way, Garrett saw a big problem. Early traffic signals switched straight from stop to go. There was no warning in between, so drivers did not have time to slow down.

Garrett invented a new kind of signal. It was a pole with arms that showed the words Stop and Go. It also had a third position that stopped traffic in every direction for a moment, so the corner could clear before anyone moved. In 1923, he received a patent for his signal. Later, he sold the rights to a large electric company.

Garrett Morgan died in 1963, but his ideas are still with us. Today's yellow light is not exactly the same as his third position, but it does the same kind of job. Every time a light turns yellow, it gives people a little extra time to be safe.

parts.title: Traffic Signals: Then and Now
paras: Have you ever waited at a red light and wished it would hurry up and turn green? That little wait keeps you safe. Traffic signals tell drivers, bike riders, and people walking when to stop and when to go. Without them, busy corners could quickly turn into a tangled mess.

About 150 years ago, city streets were crowded with horses, wagons, carriages, and people on foot. In the early 1900s, cars joined the crowd, and they moved much faster than horses. At many busy corners, a police officer stood in the middle of the street. The officer used hand signals and a whistle to tell people when to go and when to stop. It was a hard and tiring job, especially in rain or snow.

The very first traffic signal was put up in London, England, in 1868. It had two arms that moved up and down, much like the signals used for trains, and gas lamps that glowed red and green at night. A police officer had to work it by hand, and it was used for only a short time. In 1914, the first electric traffic signal lit up in Cleveland, Ohio. It had red and green lights and a buzzer to warn that the color was about to change.

Early signals had a problem. Often a light switched from green to red with no warning, and drivers did not always have time to stop. Inventors worked on ways to fix this. In 1920, a police officer named William Potts set up a light in Detroit, Michigan, with three colors: red, yellow, and green. A few years later, Garrett Morgan patented a signal with a third position that stopped traffic in all directions. Today, the yellow light warns drivers to slow down because red is coming next.

Have you noticed that red is always on top when a traffic light hangs up and down? This pattern helps everyone, including people who have trouble telling red from green. They can tell which light is on by its position.

Today, many traffic signals are run by computers. Sensors in the road can tell when a car is waiting, so a light does not stay green for an empty street. Some signals count down the seconds left to cross. Others make beeping sounds to help people who cannot see well. Most new signals use LED bulbs, which shine brightly, use less electricity, and last for years.

parts.title: The Robot That Would Not Stop
paras: Rosa and her best friend, Theo, had one week to make something for the school invention fair. Theo wanted to build a volcano. Rosa wanted to build a robot. They flipped a coin, and the robot won. Theo groaned, but he was a good sport about it.

Their robot was not fancy. Its body was a shoebox covered in silver paper, and its eyes were two bottle caps. Inside were a small motor, two wheels, and a tiny computer that Rosa's uncle helped them set up. A sensor on the front worked like a nose for bumping into things. When it sensed a wall, the robot was supposed to stop, turn, and roll away.

They named it Zero, because it cost almost zero dollars to make. Rosa typed the program, the list of steps that told Zero what to do. Go forward. If you sense something, stop. Turn left. Go forward again.

On Tuesday, Zero rolled forward, bumped the couch, and stopped. Rosa and Theo cheered. That night, Rosa added a step to make Zero turn faster, and she typed part of the program over again. On Wednesday, Zero rolled forward, bumped the couch, and kept going. It pushed against the couch with a whiny buzz, like a mosquito that would not give up. Theo laughed so hard he fell over. Rosa did not laugh.

"It's broken," she said, and her shoulders slumped as she stared at the floor. "The fair is in two days." Theo stopped laughing. He picked up Zero and turned it over. The wheels kept spinning in the air.
"Robots don't break their own rules," Theo said slowly. "They just follow the instructions we give them. So either the sensor isn't working, or the instructions are wrong."

They tested the sensor first. Rosa tapped it with a pencil, and a little green light blinked on. The sensor was fine. Then they read the program line by line, out loud, like a recipe. Halfway down, Theo pointed at the screen. Rosa had typed "If you sense something, go" instead of "stop." One tiny word had made all the difference.

Rosa fixed the word and set Zero down. The room was silent while they watched. Zero rolled forward, bumped the couch, stopped, turned, and rolled away across the rug, as calm as a cat. Rosa and Theo whooped so loudly that Rosa's grandmother came running to see what was wrong.

At the fair, Zero rolled around its cardboard maze without a single crash. People crowded around the table. A girl asked how it worked. Rosa explained the sensor, and then Theo explained the program. "And if it ever does something silly," Theo added, "check the instructions. A robot is only as smart as the people who program it."

They did not win first place. A boy with a solar-powered fan did. But when the judge handed Rosa and Theo a ribbon for Best Problem Solvers, they agreed it was even better. On the way home, Theo asked, "Next year, a volcano?" Rosa grinned. "Next year, a robot volcano."

parts.title: Robots: Machines That Follow Instructions
paras: Robots are not just in movies anymore. Some robots build cars. Some vacuum floors. Some have even rolled across Mars. Robots come in many shapes and sizes, but they all have something in common. They do jobs by following instructions.

The word robot is only about 100 years old. It first appeared in a play written in 1920 by Karel Čapek, a writer from the country now called the Czech Republic. The word comes from a Czech word that means hard work. Today, people all over the world use it.

Most robots have three main parts. Sensors gather information, the way your eyes and ears do. Some sensors notice light, sound, or touch. A computer acts like the robot's brain. It follows a program, a list of instructions written by people. Motors and other moving parts let the robot act by rolling, lifting, or grabbing. Some robots also have speakers so they can play music or talk.

Robots are very good at jobs that are boring, heavy, or dangerous for people. In car factories, robot arms lift heavy parts and join them together. They can do the same task thousands of times without getting tired. In some warehouses, robots carry boxes from shelf to shelf. Other robots dive deep into the ocean, where the water is dark and icy cold, to explore places divers cannot reach.

Some of the most famous robots explore places people cannot easily go. NASA has sent several robot rovers to Mars. A rover named Perseverance landed there in 2021. It drives over rocky ground, takes pictures, and collects bits of rock. Earlier rovers, such as Sojourner and Curiosity, explored Mars, too. Messages from Earth can take several minutes to reach Mars, so the rover uses its own sensors to steer around rocks.

Robots can seem smart, but most robots cannot think the way people do. A robot vacuum does not know it is cleaning a room. It simply follows its program: move forward, sense a wall, turn, and keep going. If the program has a mistake, the robot will follow the mistake, too. People design robots, write their programs, and fix them when something goes wrong.

Maybe someday you will build a robot of your own. Many schools have robot clubs where students build and program simple robots. All you need is a problem to solve, some patience, and a willingness to try again when your robot does something silly.

parts.title: The Squirrel and the Groundhog
paras: At the edge of a meadow, beside a little creek, lived a squirrel named Nibble and a groundhog named Mumble. Nibble was quick and clever, and she loved to talk. Mumble was slow and gentle, and he hardly ever said a word. They were neighbors, but they did almost nothing the same way.

When autumn leaves began to tumble from the trees, Nibble got busy. She raced up and down the oak trees, carrying acorns in her mouth. Then she buried them one at a time, here and there, all over the meadow. "I have a hundred hiding spots," she boasted to anyone who would listen, "and I remember every single one!"

Mumble got busy too, in his own simple way. He munched clover and sweet grass from morning until night, until his belly was as round as an apple. Then he started to dig. He dug a long tunnel under the roots of the old maple tree. At the very end, he made a snug little room and lined it with dry grass.
Nibble giggled when she peeked into his tunnel. "Mumble, you are wasting the whole fall!" she said. "You haven't saved a single nut. When winter comes, you'll be hungry and bored down in that hole."
Mumble only blinked. "I don't need nuts," he said in his slow, soft voice. "When the cold comes, I sleep."
"Sleep?" Nibble laughed so hard that her tail shook. "That's the silliest plan I ever heard! My plan is the only smart plan."
Mumble said nothing. He just yawned, waddled into his tunnel, and pulled a bundle of grass across the door.
Then winter came. The first snow drifted down like flour shaken from a sifter. By morning, the meadow was hidden under a smooth white blanket.

Nibble scampered out to find her acorns. She dug by the big rock and found one. She dug by the fence post and found only frozen dirt. Under the snow, her hundred hiding spots all looked exactly the same.

That night an icy wind roared across the meadow. It tugged at Nibble's leafy nest until the leaves blew away one by one. Shivering, with only three acorns, Nibble crept down from her tree. The only shelter she could see, the only place safe from the wind, was the hole under the maple tree.

Nibble pushed past the bundle of grass and slipped inside. The tunnel was dark, still, and surprisingly warm. Far down at the end, Mumble lay curled in a ball, taking slow, gentle breaths. He opened one sleepy eye. "Room by the door," he mumbled, and he was asleep again before she could say thank you.
Nibble curled up by the door and nibbled her three acorns. Outside, the wind howled, but inside she was safe and dry. She thought about how she had laughed at Mumble's plan, and her ears grew hot.
When the first warm days came at last, Mumble poked his nose out into the sunshine. Nibble was waiting for him. "Mumble," she said, "I'm sorry I laughed at you. Your plan kept us both warm."
Mumble smiled. "Your acorns fed you, and my long sleep kept me," he said. "There is more than one good way to get through a winter."
Moral: Do not laugh at others just because their way is different from yours.

parts.title: Ready for Winter: How Forest Animals Survive the Cold
paras: In a Virginia forest, winter can be a hard time for animals. The air turns cold, snow may cover the ground, and food becomes hard to find. Animals cannot put on a jacket or turn up the heat. Instead, they have adaptations. An adaptation is a body part or a behavior that helps a living thing survive in its habitat.

Many animals grow a thicker coat as winter gets close. A white-tailed deer trades its thin, reddish summer coat for a thick, gray-brown winter coat. Its winter hairs are hollow, so they trap warm air close to its body.
Birds stay warm in a similar way. On a cold morning, a little chickadee fluffs up its feathers until it looks like a round ball, and the air caught between the feathers holds in heat.

Some animals sleep through the hardest part of winter. This long, deep sleep is called hibernation. A groundhog spends the summer and fall eating plants until it is fat. Then it curls up in a room at the end of its underground burrow.

Once the groundhog is asleep, its body cools, and its heart slows from about 80 beats a minute to only a few. It hardly moves at all. The groundhog lives on the fat stored in its body until the warm days of spring return.

Gray squirrels do not hibernate. They stay busy all winter, so they need food they can find. In the fall, a squirrel buries acorns and other nuts one at a time in many different spots. Winter food is scarce. Fresh plants are gone and most nuts have been eaten, so the squirrel digs up its hidden supply.
A squirrel uses memory and a strong sense of smell to find its nuts. It does not find every one, and some forgotten acorns sprout into new oak trees.
Other animals leave. When the days grow shorter and food becomes hard to find, many birds fly south to warmer places where food is easy to find. This long trip is called migration.

The ruby-throated hummingbird is not much bigger than your thumb, yet many fly all the way to Mexico or Central America. Some even cross the Gulf of Mexico without stopping. In the spring, they make the long trip back north to raise their young.

Deer, groundhogs, squirrels, and hummingbirds can live in the same forest, but they meet winter in different ways. Some grow warm coats, some sleep, some store food, and some travel. Each adaptation solves the same problem: how to stay alive until spring brings warm days and plenty of food again.

parts.title: The Squirrel, the Groundhog, and the Bees
paras: One spring morning, Nibble the squirrel and Mumble the groundhog sat in the sunny corner of their meadow. Every summer, the meadow animals held a Harvest Market. Everyone brought something to share or trade, and the best treats were gone by noon. Last year, Nibble had brought acorn muffins, and Mumble had brought a basket of clover.

"This year," said Nibble, "let's grow strawberries for the market. We'll have the sweetest berries anyone has ever tasted!" Mumble nodded slowly. That was a lot of words for one morning, but he liked the plan.

So the two friends started a garden. Mumble dug the dark, crumbly soil with his strong claws. Nibble carried water from the creek in an acorn cap, one splash at a time. Every evening, they checked their plants and counted the new leaves. Soon green leaves popped up, and then the plants were covered with small white flowers.
That was when the bees arrived. They zipped from flower to flower, buzzing like tiny motors. Mumble backed away. His whiskers trembled, and he hid behind a fern. "Too noisy," he whispered.

Nibble did not like the bees either. "Shoo!" she shouted, waving a leaf. "These are OUR flowers! Go find your own!" Every morning after that, the two friends chased the bees away. They even built a fence of sticks around the garden. Soon hardly any bees came at all. Nibble was proud of the fence. "Now our garden is safe," she said.

In early summer, the berries appeared. Nibble ran to see them, and her smile drooped. The berries were tiny, hard, and lumpy, like little green pebbles. Mumble poked one with his nose and sighed. Even the few that turned red were small and sour. "What happened?" Nibble cried. "We gave them water and sunshine and good soil!"

Just then, an old bumblebee landed on the fence. Her name was Grandmother Clover, and her fuzzy coat was dusted with yellow. "You chased away your helpers," she said kindly. "When we bees visit a flower, a fine yellow dust called pollen sticks to us. We carry it to the next flower. Many plants need pollen from another flower before they can make big, sweet fruit."
Nibble's tail drooped. Mumble's ears turned pink. "We thought you were stealing," Nibble said. "We never asked what you were doing."

That afternoon, the friends pulled down the stick fence. Mumble planted clover and daisies along the edges of the garden to invite more bees. Nibble even said "Good morning" to every bee that buzzed past, though Mumble still preferred to wave from behind his fern.

The plants were still making new flowers, and this time the bees came back. They hummed through the garden all day long. Nibble counted the bees each morning, just for fun. One day she counted forty-two. By the end of summer, the new berries were plump and shiny red, as big as a squirrel's paw and sweeter than honey.

Nibble and Mumble carried three full baskets to the Harvest Market. Their berries were gone before the sun was high. Other animals asked for their secret. "Ask a bee," Nibble said with a grin. Then they saved the very best basket for Grandmother Clover and her family.
Moral: Do not chase away a helper before you find out what that helper does.

parts.title: Nature's Partners: How Plants and Animals Need Each Other
paras: Plants and animals depend on each other. To depend on something means to need it. Animals need plants for food and shelter. Many plants need animals too, even though a plant cannot ask for help. Here are some of the ways plants and animals work as partners. Some of these partners help each other in surprising ways.

When a bee lands on a flower, it drinks a sweet juice called nectar. It also gathers pollen, a fine dust that flowers make. Bees use both nectar and pollen as food. As the bee crawls around, pollen sticks to the fuzzy hairs on its body. A busy bee may visit hundreds of flowers in a single day.

When the bee flies to the next flower, some of that pollen rubs off. Many plants need pollen from another flower before they can make seeds and fruit. Because bees carry pollen, we get apples, pumpkins, and blueberries. Strawberries also grow bigger and rounder when bees visit their flowers. Bees are not the only pollen carriers. Butterflies, moths, hummingbirds, and even some bats carry pollen, too.

Plants cannot walk, so many of them need animals to carry their seeds. In the fall, squirrels and blue jays carry acorns away from oak trees and bury them. The animals come back for many acorns, but they forget some. In the spring, a forgotten acorn may sprout into a new oak tree, far from the parent tree. One squirrel may bury thousands of nuts in a single fall.

Birds help in another way. A robin swallows a berry, and later the seeds pass out of its body in its droppings, often far away. Some seeds even hitch a ride on fur. A burr has tiny hooks that grab onto a passing deer or dog and drop off somewhere new. Many fruits are sweet and colorful, which helps animals find them and eat them.

Trees give animals homes. A woodpecker uses its strong beak to carve a hole in a dead tree. After the woodpecker moves out, the hole may become a home for a bluebird, an owl, or a flying squirrel. Many insects and spiders live in the bark and leaves. Fallen logs give shelter to salamanders, beetles, and mice.

Because partners need each other, a problem for one is a problem for the other. Scientists have found fewer bees in many places in recent years. Fewer bees means less pollen gets carried, so some farms grow less fruit. People can help by planting flowers that bloom from spring to fall and by using less bug spray in gardens. Some towns even plant wildflowers along highways to help bees and butterflies. When the bees do well, the plants do well too.

parts.title: The Otter Who Laughed at the Beaver
paras: On a fast little river at the edge of a meadow lived a beaver and an otter. Beaver was a builder. From sunrise to sunset, she cut down young trees with her strong orange teeth and dragged them to the water. Otter was a player. He slid down muddy banks, tossed pebbles in the air, and floated on his back in the sun.

"Why do you work so hard?" Otter asked one morning, munching on a crayfish. "The river gives us everything we need. Stop being so serious and come play." Otter thought Beaver's work was silly. Beaver thought Otter was a little lazy.
"The river is generous now," Beaver said, patting mud onto a pile of sticks. "But rivers can change. I am building a dam so we will have a deep pond, even in a dry summer."

Otter laughed so hard that he rolled over in the water. "A dry summer! Look at all this water!" He splashed away, singing a silly song about a beaver who was afraid of sunshine. The ducks giggled. The frogs croaked along. Beaver's ears turned hot, but she kept working.

All spring, Beaver built. She wove sticks together, stuffed the cracks with mud and pebbles, and nibbled branches to just the right size. Little by little, the water behind her dam grew deeper and wider, until a quiet pond spread across one end of the meadow. In the middle, Beaver built a cozy lodge with a secret door under the water.

Then summer came, and it was dry, just as Beaver had warned. No rain fell for weeks. The sun beat down like a hot iron, and the river grew thinner and thinner. Soon it was only a trickle, a tiny stream of water that you could step across. The fish that Otter liked to chase had nowhere to swim. His favorite mud slide turned hard and cracked.

Otter wandered along the dusty riverbed, hungry and thirsty. At last he came to Beaver's pond. It was deep and cool and full of fish. Ducks paddled near the edges, and frogs sat on the lily pads. Otter stopped at the edge. He remembered his silly song, and his face felt hot.
Beaver poked her head out of the water. Otter looked down at his paws. "I laughed at your dam," he said quietly. "I was wrong. May I please swim in your pond?"
Beaver could have laughed at him the way he had laughed at her. Instead, she slapped her tail gently on the water. "Come in," she said. "There is plenty for everyone."

Otter swam and fished all afternoon. That evening, he did something he had never done before. He picked up a stick, carried it to the dam, and pressed it into place. Beaver showed him how to fill the cracks with mud. By the time the sun went down, Otter had learned that building could be a kind of fun, too. The next spring, the two friends built the dam even higher together.
Moral: Do not laugh at someone's hard work. One day, you may be glad of it.

parts.title: Beavers: Nature's Engineers
paras: Beavers are the biggest rodents in North America. Only the capybara of South America is larger. An adult beaver can weigh 40 to 60 pounds, about as much as a medium-sized dog. Thick brown fur keeps it warm and dry in cold water. Beavers spend most of their lives in and around water, and they change the land around them more than almost any other animal except people.

A beaver's four front teeth are bright orange. They get their color from iron, which also helps make them strong. The teeth never stop growing. Chewing on wood wears them down, so a beaver must keep gnawing to keep its teeth from getting too long. A beaver can chew through a thin tree in just a few minutes. Beavers eat bark, leaves, roots, and water plants. They do not eat fish.

Beavers build dams across streams to make ponds. First, they push sticks and branches into the bottom of the stream. Then they pile on more branches, stones, and plants, and they pack the cracks with mud. Water backs up behind the dam and forms a deep, still pond. A large dam can be longer than a football field. If the dam springs a leak, the beavers hurry to fix it. Scientists have found that the sound of running water helps tell beavers where to make repairs.

In the pond, beavers build a home called a lodge. It looks like a big dome of sticks and mud. The entrances are underwater, so wolves, coyotes, and bears cannot easily get in. Inside, above the water line, is a dry room where the beaver family eats, sleeps, and raises its young. In winter, when the pond freezes, beavers swim out under the ice to eat branches they stored in the mud nearby.

Beavers are excellent swimmers. Their back feet are webbed like a duck's, and they can hold their breath underwater for up to about 15 minutes. Clear eyelids cover their eyes like goggles. Their wide, flat tail helps them steer. When a beaver senses danger, it slaps its tail hard on the water. The loud smack warns other beavers to dive. On land, beavers waddle slowly, so they like to stay close to the water.

A beaver pond helps many other living things. Fish, frogs, ducks, turtles, and insects find homes in the still water. Deer and moose come to drink. In dry summers, beaver ponds can hold water when streams nearby dry up, and during floods, the wetlands around them soak up extra water. Because their dams change whole landscapes, scientists sometimes call beavers "ecosystem engineers."

parts.title: The Magpie Who Wanted Everything New
paras: High in an oak tree lived a magpie who loved new things. If a leaf in her nest turned brown, she tossed it out. If a twig cracked, she flung it to the ground. "Old things are boring," she would say, smoothing her shiny black and white feathers. "I only want the newest and the best."

At the bottom of the same oak lived Wood Rat. Wood Rat was the opposite of Magpie. He never threw anything away. When Magpie's old twigs and feathers rained down, he gathered them up and carried them into his den. "Thank you!" he called up to the branches. Magpie only rolled her eyes. She disliked the way he collected her trash.

"Why do you keep my junk?" she asked one day. "It is useless." "Nothing is useless," said Wood Rat, "if you can find a new way to use it." He showed her a cracked acorn cap that he used as a cup and a bent twig that he had turned into a spoon. Magpie laughed and flew away.

All summer, Magpie rebuilt her nest again and again. Each time, she searched for fresh twigs, bright moss, and shiny bits of string. Each time, she found something a little bit wrong and started over. Building a brand-new nest every week was hard work, and by autumn, Magpie was tired and unhappy. Worse, the young trees nearby had been stripped bare. There were hardly any good twigs left.

Then the first winter storm came roaring through the woods. The wind shook the oak, and Magpie's newest nest, built quickly with stiff, unbendable twigs that snapped instead of curving, came apart. Twig by twig, it disappeared into the dark. Magpie clung to a branch, shivering, with nowhere to sleep.

In the morning, Wood Rat found her on the ground, her feathers ruffled and her head down. He did not say, "I told you so." Instead, he invited her into his den. It was warm and dry. The walls were lined with the soft feathers she had thrown away, and the floor was covered with her old leaves. Magpie stared. "These are mine," she said in a small voice. "I thought they were worthless."
"They kept me warm all fall," said Wood Rat. "Old things still have plenty of use in them. Would you like some back?"

Wood Rat untied a bundle of old twigs, and together they dragged it up the oak. This time, Magpie did not toss out the brown leaves or the cracked twigs. She bent them, wove them, and tucked the soft feathers in between. Some twigs were too broken to use in the walls, so she reused them to fill the cracks. When she was finished, the nest was not shiny, but it was strong.

The next storm howled all night. Magpie's nest rocked and swayed, but it held together. In the morning, she peeked over the edge and called down to Wood Rat. "It's still here!" she cried. Then she added, a little shyly, "And so are my old feathers."
Moral: Take good care of what you have. Old things can be useful in new ways.

parts.title: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle
paras: Think about everything your family throws away in one week: food wrappers, old papers, empty bottles, broken toys. It adds up fast. According to a government agency called the Environmental Protection Agency, each person in the United States throws away almost 5 pounds of trash every day. That is like tossing out a bag of flour every single day! Some of that trash could have been used again.

Most trash ends up in a landfill, a huge area where garbage is buried in the ground. Some things break down quickly in a landfill, but many do not. A plastic bottle can last for hundreds of years. Landfills also take up a lot of land. That is why many people try to follow three simple words: reduce, reuse, and recycle.

To reduce means to make less. The best way to cut down on trash is to not make it in the first place. You can carry a refillable water bottle instead of buying bottled water. You can bring lunch in a reusable box instead of a paper bag. You can also turn off lights and water when you are not using them, so you waste less. Choosing things with less packaging helps, too.

To reuse means to use something again. Before you throw something away, ask yourself if it could have another job. A glass jar can hold crayons. An old T-shirt can become a cleaning rag. Old towels and blankets can be given to animal shelters to keep the animals warm. Sometimes a broken thing can be repaired instead of replaced. A loose button can be sewn back on, and a wobbly chair leg can be glued.

To recycle means to turn old materials into new products. Paper, cardboard, glass, many plastics, and metal cans can be collected, cleaned, and made into something new. Old newspapers can become cereal boxes, and recycling paper means fewer trees need to be cut down. Plastic bottles can be made into carpet or warm fleece jackets. An aluminum can that you recycle can be melted down and back on a store shelf as a new can in about two months.

One person cannot solve the trash problem alone, but small actions add up. If every student in a class reuses one bag a week, the class can save hundreds of bags in a school year. Check the rules in your town to learn what can go in the recycling bin, because not every place recycles the same things. Some schools even hold contests to see which class can make the least trash. Then make reducing, reusing, and recycling a habit.

parts.title: Meret and the Flood Marks
paras: Meret woke up on the flat roof of her family's mud-brick house, where everyone slept on hot summer nights. She rubbed her eyes and looked out. The Nile had climbed out of its banks again. Where green wheat had stood in the spring, a wide sheet of brown water now stretched all the way to the palm trees. It was the flood season, the time of year Meret liked best.

Down in the courtyard, Mother had already preheated the round clay oven, and the smell of warm bread drifted up the ladder. Meret's little brother, Kha, was chattering nonstop. "Look, a duck! Look, two ducks! Meret, do you think fish can swim right into our fields?" Meret sighed. Kha was six, and he never stopped talking.

After breakfast, the two of them carried a basket of bread and onions to Uncle Ptah. Uncle Ptah was the village scribe. He wrote letters, counted sacks of grain, and kept careful records, which meant he wrote down important facts so no one would forget them. Sometimes he let Meret practice drawing signs on a broken piece of pottery. Her owls still looked like lumpy onions, and she often misspelled words by leaving out a sign, but Uncle Ptah never laughed.

Today, Uncle Ptah was sitting with one foot wrapped in a strip of linen. "I twisted my ankle on the wet steps," he groaned. "And today of all days! Someone must read the flood marks at the river stairs." The river stairs were stone steps that led down into the water. Lines were carved into the wall beside them, one above another. By seeing how high the water reached, the village could predict whether the next harvest would be big or small.

Meret stood up straight. "I can read the marks," she said. Uncle Ptah looked at her for a long moment. Then he nodded. "Count carefully," he said. "A number that is misread is worse than no number at all."

Meret and Kha pushed a little reed boat into the flooded field. As Meret shoved off, the mud squished between her toes, as warm as bread dough. Then she poled hard and fast. The water smelled like wet earth, and the sun bounced off it in a thousand tiny sparks. Kha leaned over the side. "A frog! A heron! Meret, look at that heron's long legs!"

"Hush, Kha," Meret snapped. "I need to think." At the river stairs, she quickly counted the lines that still showed above the water. "Four lines are dry," she said, and she began to turn the boat around. But Kha tugged her arm. "That bottom one is crooked," he said. "It doesn't have a little sign next to it like the others."

Meret frowned and looked again, slowly this time. Kha was right. Every real flood mark had a small sign carved beside it, but the line she had counted had none. It was only a crack in the stone. Meret felt her cheeks grow hot. She had been in such a hurry that she had almost carried home the wrong number.

This time, Meret counted slowly, touching each mark with her finger while Kha counted out loud with her. Three lines were dry, not four. Then she scratched the number onto a pottery piece so it could not get misplaced on the way home.

Back at the house, Uncle Ptah studied the pottery and smiled. "A good flood," he said. "Not too high and not too low. The fields will be rich and black this year." Meret took a deep breath. "Kha helped," she said. "He saw the crack before I did." Kha grinned so wide that his ears seemed to wiggle.

That evening, Uncle Ptah taught them both a new sign: three wavy lines stacked one above another. "Water," he said. Meret drew it in the soft mud by the doorstep. Then she handed the stick to Kha. "Your turn," she said. "And take your time."

parts.title: The Nile: Then and Now
paras: The Nile River flows north through northeastern Africa for about 4,100 miles until it reaches the Mediterranean Sea. Do not let a map mislead you: because north is at the top of most maps, the Nile seems to flow "up." Many people call it the longest river in the world, although some scientists think the Amazon River may be a little longer. Since prehistoric times, people have lived along its banks, because the Nile brings water to a land that is mostly desert.

Long ago, the Nile flooded every summer. Heavy rains fell far to the south, in the mountains of what is now Ethiopia, and the extra water rushed downstream into Egypt. For several months, the river spread over the fields beside it. When the water went back down, it left a layer of rich black mud called silt. Silt made the soil fertile, so crops such as wheat, barley, and flax grew tall and strong. The ancient Egyptians even called their land Kemet, which means "the black land."

Because the flood mattered so much, the ancient Egyptians divided their year into three seasons: the flood, the growing time, and the harvest. They also built Nilometers, which were stairs or walls with marks for measuring the water. A flood that was too low meant dry fields and less food. A flood that was too high could wash away houses. By reading the marks, officials could predict how good the harvest would be. Many historians think officials also used the marks to decide how much grain farmers owed in taxes.

In ancient times, the Nile was Egypt's main road. Boats made of papyrus reeds or wood carried people, animals, grain, and even giant blocks of stone for building. Sailors used a clever trick. The river's current carried boats north, and the wind usually blew from the north. So to travel south, sailors simply raised their sails and let the wind push them upstream.

Today, the Nile no longer floods Egypt every year. In 1970, Egypt finished building the Aswan High Dam. The dam holds back the river and stores water in Lake Nasser, one of the largest human-made lakes in the world. Because of the dam, farmers can water their crops all year long, and the rushing water helps make electricity. However, most of the silt now settles behind the dam instead of spreading over the fields. As a result, many farmers use fertilizer to help their crops grow.

Some things have not changed. Most people in Egypt still live close to the Nile, and the huge city of Cairo sits on its banks. Sailboats called feluccas still glide across the water, though many now carry visitors instead of grain. The Nile and the rivers that feed it flow nonstop through about eleven countries, and all of them depend on its water. Long ago and today, the Nile gives life to the land around it.
