parts.title: Kallia and the Basket of Fish
paras: Before the sun was up, Kallia and her grandfather led their gray donkey down the dusty road into Athens. Four clay jars of olive oil rocked gently in the baskets on the donkey's back. Grandfather had pressed the oil himself from the olives on their hillside farm. It was so fresh that it smelled like cut grass.

The agora was already buzzing. Under the long stoa, a covered walkway lined with stone columns, sellers spread out their goods in the shade. One woman stacked round cheeses. A boy called out, "Figs! Sweet, sticky figs!" Next to their spot, Demetrios the potter set out painted cups and bowls in careful rows. "I am stuck here until sunset," he grumbled, "and by then the fish sellers will be gone. My family will have no fish for supper again."

Grandfather looked worried. "Today we must sell our oil," he said quietly. "Our old storage jars are cracked and useless, and the olive harvest begins next week. I promised Demetrios silver coins for new jars before sunset. Without new jars, we will have nowhere to keep this year's oil."

All morning, customers came and went. A cook bought one jar and paid with a silver coin stamped with a wide-eyed owl, the symbol of Athens. A woman bought a second jar and paid with small coins. Grandfather popped one tiny coin into his cheek to keep it safe, the way many Athenians did. Kallia giggled. "Pappous, you look like you are hiding an olive in there!"
By afternoon, two jars were still unsold, and the shadows of the columns were growing long. Grandfather counted his coins and sighed. "Not enough," he said. Kallia felt her hopeful smile slip away.

Just then, a young fisherman named Nikias stopped at their stall. He carried a basket of shiny fish that still smelled of the sea. "I would love a jar of your oil," he said, "but I have no coins left today. Would you trade it for fish?"
Grandfather shook his head kindly. "I am sorry, friend. Fish will not pay the potter." Nikias nodded and walked slowly away, his shoulders drooping.

Kallia's mind raced. Fish will not pay the potter, she thought. Or would it? She remembered Demetrios grumbling about supper. "Wait here, Pappous!" she cried. She dashed across the agora, weaving carefully between baskets of figs and stacks of cheese.

"Demetrios," she panted, "if we bring you a basket of fresh fish along with our coins, would that pay for the new jars?" The potter's eyes lit up. "Fresh fish? Today? Child, that would be the best payment I have had all month!"

Kallia raced back and caught up with Nikias near the fountain. A few minutes later, the fisherman walked off happily with a jar of oil, and Kallia carried his basket of fish to the potter's stall. Grandfather handed over his coins, and Demetrios handed over four strong new jars without a single crack. Just before sunset, a baker bought their last jar of oil.

On the road home, the new jars clinked softly on the donkey's back. "You were very helpful today," Grandfather said, and he gave Kallia the tiny coin from his cheek. "You listened to what each person needed. That is the secret of a good trade." Kallia wrinkled her nose and laughed. "Thank you, Pappous. But next time, could you keep it in a bag?"

parts.title: Markets and Money: Then and Now
paras: Have you ever paid for a snack or watched a grown-up pay at a store? Buying, selling, and swapping things is called trade, and people have been trading for thousands of years. Markets long ago were different from stores today in many ways. But they were also alike in some surprising ways. Learning how people traded long ago can help us understand how we shop today.

Long ago, before there were coins, people often bartered. To barter means to trade goods for other goods without using money. A farmer with extra grain might trade it for a goat or a cooking pot. Bartering was useful, but it had a big problem. What if the potter did not want grain? The farmer would have to keep searching until he found someone who had what he needed and also wanted what he had.

Coins helped solve this problem. Many historians think the first coins were made more than 2,600 years ago in Lydia, a kingdom in what is now the country of Turkey. With coins, a farmer could sell grain to anyone who wanted it and then use the coins to buy whatever he needed. Coins were also small and easy to carry. Soon the Greeks were making coins, too. In Athens, silver coins were stamped with an owl, a symbol of the city. A coin called a drachma was worth six smaller coins called obols.

In ancient Athens, the busiest place in town was the agora, an open market and meeting place. Sellers set up stalls full of olive oil, figs, fish, cheese, honey, pottery, and cloth. Long covered walkways called stoas gave shoppers shade. City officials checked that sellers used honest weights and measures, so buyers would not be cheated. Shoppers could also visit money changers, who sat at tables and swapped coins from other cities. Old Greek plays even joke that some shoppers carried small coins safely in their mouths!

Today, most people shop in grocery stores, at malls, or online. Instead of paying only with coins, we use paper money, cards, and even phones. Store shelves hold food from all over the world, and a computer at the register quickly adds up the prices. Many stores use bar codes, little patterns of black lines that a scanner can read in a flash. Online shopping lets people buy things without ever leaving home.

Even so, markets today are a lot like the agora. At farmers markets, sellers still set up stalls outdoors, and neighbors still stop to chat. Inspectors still check that store scales are correct, just as officials did in Athens. People even still barter. When two friends swap stickers or trading cards, they are bartering, just like the farmer with his grain. Some towns even hold swap meets where neighbors trade toys, books, and clothes. Long ago and today, markets bring people together.

parts.title: Awa and the Salt Caravan
paras: Awa lived in Timbuktu, a city of sandy streets and mud-brick houses at the edge of the great desert. Her father was a copier of books. All day he sat in their shady courtyard, dipping his pen into ink and copying old books by hand, letter by careful letter. People came from far away to buy his books, because his writing was the neatest in the city.

One morning, her father laid twelve fresh pages on a mat in the sun. "The ink is still wet," he said. "A teacher is coming tonight to buy this book. I must go to the market for more paper. Will you watch the pages until the ink is dry?" Awa nodded. It was the most important job he had ever given her.

For a while, Awa sat beside the pages, humming. A lizard ran up the wall. The sun climbed higher. Then, from far away, she heard drums and shouting. Her friend Musa poked his head over the courtyard wall. "The salt caravan is here!" he cried. "Hundreds of camels! Come and see!"
Awa looked at the pages. The ink was almost dry, and the air was still. "Just a quick look," she told herself. "I will be back before anyone knows I was gone." She ran out the gate after Musa.

The market was the noisiest place Awa had ever seen. Camels grunted and groaned as they knelt in the dust. Each one carried two huge slabs of salt, one on each side, as white as clouds. Traders shouted out prices, and coins clinked into wooden bowls. Everywhere, people were bargaining, arguing back and forth until they agreed on a fair price. A trader from the south weighed tiny piles of gold dust on a shiny brass scale.

Awa forgot all about the time. Then a gust of hot wind whipped across the market. Dust swirled up from the ground, and people pulled their scarves over their faces. Awa's heart jumped. The wind! The pages!

She ran home faster than she had ever run in her life. The courtyard was a mess. Pages lay scattered across the ground, and one was stuck against the wall. With shaking hands, Awa gathered them up and counted. Ten, eleven. Only eleven. One page was missing.

Awa searched every corner of the courtyard. She searched the street outside. At last she found the twelfth page caught in a thorny bush two houses away. It was dusty, but it was not torn. She brushed it off as gently as she could, but a gray smudge stayed in one corner.

When her father came home, Awa could have said nothing. Instead, she took a deep breath and told him everything. He looked at the smudged page for a long time. "I am sad that you left the pages," he said at last. "But you told me the truth, and that makes me proud." He showed her how to rub away most of the dust with a soft cloth.

The next morning, her father laid out new pages to dry. This time, Awa set a small, smooth stone on the corner of each one. Then she sat beside them all morning, even when the drums began again. In the afternoon, her father let her dip the pen in the ink. Slowly, carefully, she wrote her name for the very first time.
Awa looked at the dark, curving letters. Salt and gold filled the market, but she thought the greatest treasure in Timbuktu might be the words.

parts.title: Mali: Then and Now
paras: Long ago, one of the richest empires in the world grew up in West Africa. It was called the Mali Empire. It began in the 1200s, and at its largest, it stretched more than 1,000 miles, from the Atlantic Ocean far inland along the Niger River. Many historians think it was one of the biggest empires of its time. Its cities were filled with traders, teachers, and builders, and its markets were full of goods from faraway places.

Mali grew rich from trade. In the south, people dug gold out of the ground. In the Sahara Desert to the north, workers cut salt from the earth in big slabs. People everywhere needed salt to keep food from spoiling and to stay healthy in the hot weather. Long lines of camels called caravans carried the salt south across the sandy desert. In Mali's busy markets, traders swapped gold for salt, and the rulers of Mali collected taxes on the trade.

The most famous ruler of Mali was Mansa Musa. Mansa means king. In 1324, he made a long journey across the desert to Egypt and beyond. Thousands of people traveled with him, and camels carried huge loads of gold. Musa gave away so much gold in the city of Cairo, Egypt, that writers there said its price dropped for years. Stories of his riches spread all the way to Europe. One mapmaker drew Mansa Musa on a map, sitting on a throne and holding a large piece of gold.

Under Mansa Musa and the rulers after him, the city of Timbuktu became a center of learning. Students came from far away to study math, science, medicine, law, and poetry. Scholars wrote and copied books by hand, and families stored them carefully in their homes for hundreds of years. Today, many thousands of these old handwritten books, called manuscripts, still survive. People are working hard to protect them and share them with the world.

Builders in Mali used what they had all around them: mud. They mixed earth, water, and straw, shaped it into bricks, and dried the bricks in the sun. In the town of Djenné stands the largest mud-brick building in the world. Rain wears away a little of its outside every year. So once a year, the whole town gathers to spread a fresh coat of mud on its walls. It is a noisy, happy festival, with music and races to see who can carry mud the quickest.

Today, Mali is a country in West Africa. Its capital is Bamako, a busy city on the Niger River. Many people in Mali farm, fish, or raise animals. Some old ways continue, too. Camel caravans still carry slabs of salt from mines in the desert to Timbuktu, just as they did hundreds of years ago. The trip across the hot, sandy desert can take weeks.

parts.title: Julia Reads the Road
paras: Julia had been riding in the cart since sunrise, and she was unhappy about it. The wooden wheels rattled nonstop over the paving stones, bump, bump, bump, until her teeth chattered. The sun was hot. Her little brother, Lucius, had fallen asleep on a sack of grain and was snoring like a tiny pig. "How much farther to Rome?" Julia asked for the tenth time.

"Grandmother's house is a long way yet," Mother said. "Try to be patient." Julia sighed and flopped back against the bags. She felt restless, as if her arms and legs wanted to do anything except sit still. She counted the clouds. She counted the trees. She even counted the bumps, until she lost track at four hundred.

Father turned around on the driver's bench. "You don't have to keep asking," he said. "The road will tell you. Watch for the tall stones beside it." He pointed. A round stone post, as tall as Julia, stood at the edge of the road. Letters were carved into it. Julia had seen these stones all morning, but she had never wondered what they were.

"That is a milestone," Father explained. "The builders of this road set one up every mile. Each one tells how many miles it is to Rome. See those marks? An X means ten. A V means five. Each I means one." Julia squinted at the stone. Under the word ROMA, she saw XXIII.
"Ten and ten is twenty," she said slowly, "and one, two, three more. Twenty-three miles!" "Exactly," said Father.

After that, the trip seemed to move more quickly. Julia stood up in the cart to watch for each new stone. XXII. XXI. XX. She called out the numbers so loudly that Lucius woke up and joined in, even though he could not read them. Travelers passed by on horses and on foot. Some walked beside donkeys loaded with baskets. Soldiers marched past in a neat line, their sandals slapping the stones. It was the busiest road Julia had ever seen.

In the afternoon, they came to a place where a smaller road split off to the left. A traveler resting under a pine tree called out to them. "Going to Rome? Take the left road. It's shorter!" Father slowed the mule. Mother sounded unsure. "Are you certain?" she asked Father. "We have never come this way before."

Julia remembered what Father had said: the road will tell you. She looked for a milestone, and there was one beside each road. The stone beside the big road said ROMA XII. The stone beside the left road had a different name carved on it, a name Julia did not know. Under that name were the letters VI.

Julia read both stones twice to make sure she had not misread them. "Father!" she cried. "The left road doesn't go to Rome. It goes somewhere else, six miles away. Our road says Rome, twelve miles." Father read the stones himself, and then he smiled. "The traveler must not have understood where we were going," he said. "Good thing someone was watching carefully."

They stayed on the wide stone road. As the sun sank lower, the stones counted down. V. IV. III. II. Lucius fell asleep again, but Julia did not. She wanted to see every single stone. At last she saw the city walls glowing gold in the evening light, bigger than anything she had imagined.
Grandmother was waiting at her door. She hugged them all, and then she asked Julia, "Was it a long, boring trip?" Julia grinned. "No," she said. "I read the whole road."

parts.title: Roman Roads: Then and Now
paras: About 2,000 years ago, the Romans ruled a huge empire that stretched across Europe, North Africa, and parts of the Middle East. To hold it together, they needed a way to move soldiers, messengers, and goods quickly from place to place. Their answer was roads, and they built a lot of them. Historians think the Romans built more than 50,000 miles of paved roads, enough to wrap around Earth twice. Soldiers often built the roads themselves.

Roman roads were built in layers, like a giant sandwich. First, workers dug a long, deep trench. Next, they filled it with layers of large stones, smaller stones, and gravel, packing down each layer. On top, they fitted big, flat paving stones tightly together. Workers used simple tools, such as shovels, picks, and baskets. Building a road this way took many workers and a lot of time, but the roads were strong enough to last for hundreds of years.

Roman builders were careful planners. They made each road a little higher in the middle than at the edges, like the top of a loaf of bread. When it rained, water ran off to the sides instead of making puddles in the middle. Many roads also had ditches along the sides to carry the water away. Even so, workers sometimes had to rebuild parts of a road after a flood. Roman roads were also as straight as possible, because the shortest way between two places is a straight line.

Along the major roads, the Romans set up milestones, tall stone posts that told travelers how far they had come or how far they had to go. A Roman mile was 1,000 paces, or about 2,000 steps. That is a little shorter than the mile we use today. In the city of Rome, a golden milestone stood near the center of the city. Some people think this is where the saying "All roads lead to Rome" comes from.

The most famous Roman road is the Appian Way. Work on it began in 312 BCE, more than 2,300 years ago. It ran south from Rome for hundreds of miles. The Romans called it the queen of roads. Travelers on the Appian Way passed farms, inns, and stone monuments. Some parts of it are still there today, and people can walk on the very same stones that Romans walked on long ago.

Many Roman roads have disappeared under fields and cities, but their paths live on. In parts of Europe, modern highways follow the same routes the Romans chose. Some Roman bridges are still used by cars and people today, and visitors can see old milestones in museums. Engineers still use Roman ideas, too. The next time you see a road that is higher in the middle, think of the Roman builders who used that idea long ago.

parts.title: Hare and the Runaway Shadow
paras: Gather close, and I will tell you a tale from the land of tall grass. Is it true? Is it not? Listen, and you decide.

Long ago, on a wide, grassy plain, there stood one great baobab tree. Its trunk was as wide as a house, and its branches spread out like the arms of a grandmother. In the dry season, the sun blazed down so fiercely that the grass turned the color of straw and the ground burned like a cooking pot. Every afternoon, all the animals came to rest in the cool shade beneath the tree.

All the animals, that is, until Hyena decided the shade was his. One bright morning, he stretched out under the tree and showed his teeth. "This tree is mine," he growled. "Its shade is mine. Anyone who wants to sit here must bring me a gift. Bring me a fat melon or a sweet honeycomb, or stay out in the sun!"

The animals were dismayed. Their faces fell, and their ears drooped. Gazelle had no melons. Tortoise had no honey. Little Mongoose had nothing at all. For three long days, they stood in the hot sun, panting, while Hyena snored in the shade with his belly full of gifts.

Now, Hare was small, but she was clever, and she had been watching the tree's shadow for many days. She had noticed something Hyena had not. So the next morning, just as the sun peeked over the hills, she hopped up to him and gave a polite bow.
"Great Hyena," she said, "you are mighty indeed. But look over there. Your shadow is running away!"

Hyena lifted his head. It was true. In the early light, most of the tree's shadow was not under the tree at all. It stretched far across the grass, long and thin, almost to the river. "Everyone knows that whoever holds the tip of a shadow holds the whole shadow," said Hare. "If you do not guard the tip, someone might steal it."

Hyena leaped up. "Nobody steals from me!" He raced to the very tip of the shadow and sat down on it, holding on tight. But as the sun climbed higher, the shadow began to shrink. Inch by inch, its tip slid back toward the trunk and left Hyena sitting in the bright, hot sunlight. Hyena had to scramble after it, and every time he caught up, it crept away again.

While Hyena was busy at the tip, the other animals tiptoed into the shade near the trunk. Oh, how cool it felt after the burning sun! Gazelle let out a sigh of delight. Tortoise tucked in his tired feet. Little Mongoose curled up and fell fast asleep.

At midday, the sun stood high overhead, and the shadow shrank into a small dark puddle around the trunk. Hyena sat at its very edge, his tongue hanging out. "Hold on tight," Hare called. "It will run again soon." And it did. All afternoon, the shadow stretched the other way, toward the hills, and Hyena chased its tip across the hot grass.

As the sun sank low, the shadow grew longer and longer. At last, the sun slipped below the edge of the plain, the whole plain turned gray, and the shadow was gone. Hyena flopped down, too tired to stand. "Someone stole my shadow!" he wailed.

Hare hopped over and sat beside him. "Nobody stole it," she said kindly. "A shadow belongs to the sun and the tree. It moves for everyone, and no one can hold it in his paws. You spent the whole day chasing something you could never keep, while the rest of us shared the cool."

Hyena was too tired to argue. The next day, he lay down in the shade beside the others and did not ask for a single melon. And that is why, the old ones say, a hyena trots across the plain in the heat of the day. He is still looking for the shadow he tried to keep.

parts.title: Sunlight and Shadows
paras: Step outside on a sunny day, and you will notice two things: bright light all around you and a dark shape stuck to your feet. The light comes from the sun, a star about 93 million miles away. The dark shape is your shadow. Sunlight and shadows may seem simple, but they help explain why some places feel hot, why others feel cool, and even why the wind blows.

Light travels in straight lines. When sunlight hits something it cannot pass through, such as a tree, a house, or your body, the light is blocked. The light cannot bend around the object, so a dark area forms on the other side. That dark area is a shadow. Because the object is between the sun and the ground, a shadow always points away from the sun. Try it at night with a flashlight. Hold your hand between the light and a wall, and a hand-shaped shadow will appear on the wall.

If you watch a shadow all day, you will see it change. In the morning, the sun is low in the eastern sky, so shadows are long and stretch toward the west. As the sun climbs higher, shadows get shorter. Around midday, when the sun is highest, shadows are at their shortest. In the late afternoon, the sun sinks low in the west, and shadows grow long again, this time stretching toward the east. The shadow is not really moving on its own. It changes because Earth is turning, so the sun seems to move across the sky.

Sunlight carries heat as well as light. When a tree blocks the sun, it blocks some of that heat, too. That is why the shade under a tree feels cooler than the sunny ground nearby. Some surfaces get hotter than others. Dark blacktop can absorb a lot of sunlight, soaking it up and turning it into heat. On a summer afternoon, it can get hot enough to hurt bare feet. Light-colored surfaces bounce more sunlight away, so they stay cooler. On hot days, people and animals often look for shade for this very reason.

The sun does more than warm your face. It drives the weather. Sunlight does not heat Earth evenly. Land heats up faster than water, and a bare field heats up faster than a shady forest. The air above a warm place gets warm, too, and warm air rises. Cooler air then moves in to take its place. That moving air is wind. This is one reason a breeze often blows in from the ocean on a sunny afternoon at the beach. The sun also warms oceans, lakes, and puddles and turns some of the water into an invisible gas. Later, that water can form clouds and fall as rain.

Long before clocks, people used shadows to tell time. A sundial has a flat face with marks around the edge and a pointer that sticks up. As the sun moves across the sky, the pointer's shadow slides from mark to mark like the hand of a clock. People in ancient Egypt used shadow clocks more than three thousand years ago. You can make a shadow clock, too. Stand a pencil in a lump of clay in a sunny spot, and mark the tip of its shadow every hour. What do you notice by late afternoon?

parts.title: Reading the Clouds
paras: Look up on almost any day, and you will see clouds. Some look like heaps of cotton. Some look like a gray blanket pulled across the sky. Others look like thin white feathers. Clouds are not just pretty to look at. If you know how to read them, they can give you clues about the weather that is on its way.

A cloud is made of billions of tiny drops of water or tiny bits of ice. Each droplet is so small and light that it floats in the air. The water in a cloud comes from oceans, lakes, rivers, and even puddles that the sun has warmed. Clouds form when warm, moist air rises. As the air goes higher, it cools. Cooler air cannot hold as much water vapor, the invisible gas form of water. So some of the vapor turns into droplets on tiny specks of dust, salt, or smoke. When billions of droplets gather, you can see them as a cloud. Thin clouds look white because sunlight shines through them. Very thick clouds look gray because less light can get through.

Cumulus clouds are the puffy ones with flat bottoms and rounded tops. Their name comes from a Latin word that means heap or pile. On a sunny day, small cumulus clouds usually mean fair weather. But keep watching. On a hot afternoon, a cumulus cloud can keep growing taller and taller. Warm air keeps rushing up inside it, piling the cloud higher, the way a baker piles frosting on a cake.

Stratus clouds are flat, gray layers that can cover the whole sky like a blanket. They hang low, and they often bring a gloomy day with drizzle, a light rain of very fine drops. When a stratus cloud forms right down at the ground, we call it fog. If you have ever walked through fog, you have walked inside a cloud!

Cirrus clouds are thin, wispy streaks that look like strands of hair or feathers. They float very high in the sky, where the air is so cold that they are made of ice instead of water. Cirrus clouds do not bring rain themselves. However, when more and more of them spread across the sky, they can be a sign that the weather may change in a day or so. Sailors long ago watched for these feathery streaks before setting out to sea.

When a cumulus cloud grows very tall, it can become a cumulonimbus cloud, the cloud that makes thunderstorms. Nimbus is a Latin word for rain cloud. These giant clouds have dark bottoms, and some grow taller than the highest mountains on Earth. Their tops often spread out flat. A cumulonimbus cloud can bring heavy rain, strong winds, thunder, lightning, and sometimes hail. If you see one building, it is time to head inside.

More than two hundred years ago, a scientist in England named Luke Howard loved to watch the sky. He sorted clouds into groups and gave them Latin names. Scientists all over the world still use his names today. The next time you go outside, look up and try to read the clouds yourself. Are they puffy, flat, wispy, or towering? What do you think they are telling you?

parts.title: How Wind Found Its Work
paras: Long, long ago, when the world was still new, Sky had four children. Sun was the oldest. Her job was to give the world light and warmth. Rain watered the plants and filled the rivers. Snow tucked the sleeping fields under a soft white blanket each winter. But Wind, the youngest, had no job at all.

Wind did not mind at first. He was fast and strong, and he loved to show off. He raced across the grasslands, flattening the grass. He whistled through the canyons just to hear his own voice. He spun the dust into little whirlwinds and chased the clouds across the sky. "Look how powerful I am!" he would boast. "I am the strongest of all Sky's children!"

But Wind's play caused trouble. He blew the hats right off the farmers' heads. He tipped over baskets of berries and sent the berries rolling down the hill. When he raced across the lake, he whipped up waves so high that the fishing boats rocked and bobbed like corks. When he roared through the forest, the old trees groaned, and pieces of their bark flew off.
"Wind, please stop!" the animals and people cried. "You are too rough! Go away and leave us alone!"

Wind's feelings were hurt. He had only been playing. His cheeks burned, and he could not look at anyone. He flew far away to a deep, dark cave in the mountains, curled up, and refused to come out. "Fine," he grumbled. "If they don't want me, I will rest here forever."

At first, everyone was glad. The days were calm and quiet. But soon, strange things began to happen. Summer came, and the hot air sat still and heavy over the land. People fanned themselves with leaves, but it did not help. Out on the lake, the boats with sails could not move at all. The rain clouds stayed piled up over one valley, so that valley flooded while the rest of the land turned dry and dusty. And under every tree, seeds lay in heaps on the ground, too crowded to grow.

Old Tortoise, the wisest creature in the land, set off slowly up the mountain. It took him many long, hot days. Tortoise was slow, but he never stopped. At last he reached the cave and poked his head inside. "Wind," he said, "the world needs you."
"No, it doesn't," Wind sniffed. "Everyone told me to go away."
"They told you to stop being rough," said Tortoise. "That is not the same as telling you to stop being Wind. Your strength is a gift. Use it gently, and go where you are needed."

Wind thought about this for a long time. Then he slipped out of the cave, as softly as a sigh. He drifted down to the hot valley and blew a cool, light breeze across the farmers' faces. They looked up and smiled. He swept the heavy clouds away from the flooded valley and carried them to the dry fields, where the rain fell gently. He filled the sails of the fishing boats and pushed them home. Then he scooped up the crowded seeds and scattered them far and wide, so that new trees and flowers could grow.

This time, nobody told Wind to go away. Children ran outside to fly their kites, and the farmers waved their hats in the air to thank him. The fishing families sang as their boats sailed home. Even Old Tortoise smiled as the breeze tickled his wrinkled neck.

And so Wind found his work. Ever since, he has carried clouds, cooled the land, and spread seeds across the earth. Sometimes, it is true, he forgets and plays too rough. But most days, if you stand still and listen, you can hear him whispering through the leaves, busy at the job he was given long ago.

parts.title: Wind: Air on the Move
paras: You cannot see wind, but you can see what it does. It makes flags flap, leaves rustle, and kites climb into the sky. On a calm day, smoke rises straight up from a chimney. On a windy day, it bends sideways and blows away. Wind is simply air that is moving from one place to another.

Wind begins with the sun. The sun does not warm Earth evenly. Land, water, forests, and deserts all heat up differently, and the air above them heats up differently, too. Warm air is lighter than cool air, so it rises, like a hot-air balloon. Then cooler air rushes in to take its place. That rushing air is wind. The bigger the difference in temperature, the stronger the wind can blow.

You can feel this happen at the beach. On a sunny day, the land heats up faster than the water. Warm air rises over the sand, and cool air from the ocean blows in to replace it. This cool wind is called a sea breeze. It is one reason the beach can feel cooler than places farther from the water on a hot afternoon. At night, the land cools off faster than the water, and the breeze often turns around and blows out toward the sea.

Weather scientists, called meteorologists, use tools to study the wind. A wind vane shows which direction the wind is coming from. Its arrow points into the wind, so a north wind makes the arrow point north. An anemometer measures how fast the wind is blowing. It has little cups that catch the wind and spin around. The faster the cups spin, the stronger the wind. Some airports use a windsock, a cloth tube that fills with air and shows which way the wind is blowing.

Wind speed is measured in miles per hour. A gentle breeze might blow at about 5 miles per hour, just enough to rustle leaves. One of the fastest winds ever measured on land was a gust of 231 miles per hour. It was recorded in 1934 at the top of Mount Washington in New Hampshire, where scientists still measure the weather every day.

Wind is one of nature's busiest workers. It carries clouds from place to place, bringing rain to dry land. It scatters seeds, like the fluffy seeds of dandelions, so new plants can grow in new places. It cools us on hot days. Over thousands of years, wind can even shape rocks by blasting them with tiny grains of sand. Wind is not always gentle, though. Strong winds can knock down trees, so meteorologists warn people when a big storm is coming.

People have used the wind for thousands of years. Long ago, sailors raised sails to let the wind push their boats across the sea. Windmills used wind to grind grain into flour and to pump water. Today, tall wind turbines with giant blades turn wind into electricity. A single turbine can make enough electricity for hundreds of homes, and wind power does not make smoke.

parts.title: Why the Rain Comes Back
paras: In the very first days of the world, water only knew how to go one way: down. Rain fell once, at the beginning of time, and after that, every drop rolled downhill. Streams ran into rivers, rivers ran into the sea, and nothing ever came back up. Year after year, the rivers grew thinner, the ponds shrank, and the land grew thirsty.

In a village beside a drying river lived a girl named Tala. Every morning she walked farther and farther to fill her family's water jar. One morning she found the riverbed cracked and empty, with only a few frogs sitting sadly in the mud. "The sea has all the water," Tala said. "Someone has to bring it back."

So Tala went to ask the Sun. She climbed to the top of the highest hill, where the Sun rested at dawn before starting across the sky. Her legs ached and her throat was dry, but she did not turn back. "Great Sun," she said, "the land is dying of thirst. Will you help us bring the water back from the sea?"

The Sun thought for a moment. "I can warm the sea," she said, "and my warmth can lift the water into the air. But it will rise as a vapor, so thin and light that no one can see it or hold it. It will drift away, and it will not fall as rain. Someone must gather it."

Tala thanked the Sun and climbed higher, all the way to the cold, quiet rooftop of the sky, where Sky Grandmother sat at her loom. Sky Grandmother had wrinkled hands and a shawl of stars, and she could weave anything. "Grandmother," Tala said, "the Sun will lift the water from the sea. Can you catch it?"

Sky Grandmother smiled. "Up here, the air is cold," she said. "When the warm vapor reaches me, the cold will squeeze it into tiny droplets, smaller than grains of sand. I will gather them and weave them into clouds. But my clouds are heavy and slow. They cannot travel to the land by themselves."

"Then I will find someone who travels," said Tala. She hurried down the mountain to the place where Wind lived, whistling and restless. When Tala explained the plan, Wind laughed and spun her around. "Finally, a job worthy of me!" he said. "I will carry the clouds wherever they are needed."

And so they began. The Sun warmed the wide blue sea, and invisible vapor rose like a sigh. High above, Sky Grandmother caught it in her cold hands and wove soft white clouds, one after another. Wind pushed the clouds across the sky toward the thirsty land. The clouds grew fat and gray as they gathered more and more droplets. When they were too heavy to hold any more, the droplets joined into raindrops and fell.

Tala was standing in the dry riverbed when the first drop hit her nose. Then another fell, and another, until rain came pouring down, drumming on the rooftops and splashing into the cracks of the earth. The frogs croaked for joy. The villagers ran outside and danced in the mud. The river woke up and began to run again, rushing all the way down to the sea.
"But won't the water all run away again?" Tala's little brother asked.
Tala laughed. "It will," she said. "And then the Sun will lift it again, and Sky Grandmother will weave it again, and Wind will carry it again. It will go around and around forever."

That is why, the old people say, the rain always comes back. The water in your cup has been in the sea, in the clouds, and in the rivers many, many times. Each part of the circle depends on the others. If even one of them stopped working, the whole world would be thirsty again.

parts.title: Around and Around: The Water Cycle
paras: Earth has been reusing the same water for billions of years. The total amount of water on Earth stays about the same, and very little ever leaves our planet. The water you drank today may once have been part of an ocean wave, a snowflake on a mountain, or even a puddle that a dinosaur splashed through. That is because water moves in a never-ending loop called the water cycle. The sun powers the whole thing.

The water cycle has no real beginning or end, but a good place to start is the ocean. Oceans cover about 70 percent of Earth's surface and hold about 97 percent of its water. When the sun warms the ocean, some of the water turns into an invisible gas called water vapor and rises into the air. This change is called evaporation. Water also evaporates from lakes, rivers, puddles, and wet clothes on a clothesline. The warmer it is, the faster water evaporates, which is why puddles dry up quickly on a sunny afternoon.

Plants add water vapor to the air, too. They pull water up from the soil through their roots, and some of it escapes through tiny holes in their leaves. A big oak tree can give off about 100 gallons of water on a hot summer day.

As water vapor rises, the air around it gets colder. Cold air cannot hold as much water vapor as warm air, so the vapor turns back into tiny droplets of liquid water. This change is called condensation. The droplets gather on bits of dust in the air, and billions of them together form a cloud. Fog is simply a cloud that forms close to the ground. You can see condensation at home, too. On a hot day, drops of water form on the outside of a glass of ice water. Those drops came from water vapor in the air.

Inside a cloud, the tiny droplets bump into each other and join together. They grow bigger and heavier. When they become too heavy to float, they fall to Earth as precipitation. Precipitation can be rain, snow, sleet, or hail, depending on how cold the air is. In very cold clouds, water freezes into ice crystals that can fall as snow.

When precipitation reaches the ground, it collects in many places. Some flows across the land into streams and rivers, which carry it back to lakes and the ocean. Water that flows over the ground like this is called runoff. Some soaks into the ground, where it becomes groundwater that plant roots and wells can reach. Some is frozen in glaciers and ice caps and may stay there for thousands of years. Then the sun warms the water, and the cycle starts again.

Because of the water cycle, Earth does not run out of water, but most of it is too salty to drink. Less than 1 percent of all Earth's water is fresh water that people can easily use from lakes, rivers, and the ground. That is why it is important to keep water clean and not waste it. Every drop is part of a journey that has been going on for billions of years.
